string-array.name: daily_learning_tips
string-array.item: Learn five to seven new words at a time and use each one in a sentence.
Review new words after a day, a week, and a month to strengthen memory.
Say your answer aloud before tapping the button to train active speech.
Read a short English text aloud for at least five minutes today.
Do not translate every word; try to understand the main idea first.
Save useful word combinations instead of isolated words.
After a mistake, create one new example using the same rule.
Listen to a short recording twice: first without text, then with text.
Switch your phone to English for a few hours each week.
Repeat difficult sentences slowly, then increase your speed.
Learn a suitable article together with every new countable noun.
Compare Present Perfect and Past Simple using events from your life.
Keep your daily streak even when you only have five minutes.
Split a long sentence into meaningful chunks and rebuild it.
Notice verb endings instead of focusing only on familiar vocabulary.
Summarize a short video in three simple English sentences.
Ask yourself questions in English and answer in complete phrases.
Learn irregular verbs in small groups with similar patterns.
Review the rule before a test and analyze every mistake afterward.
Use one new word at least three times in different contexts today.
Listen at a comfortable speed before trying faster speech.
Learn prepositions inside phrases: interested in, good at, depend on.
Read a news headline and predict what the article will say.
Keep a list of words you confuse and compare them in pairs.
Write a tiny journal entry: three sentences about your day are enough.
Practice word order separately in questions and negative sentences.
Watch a familiar film with English subtitles instead of translated ones.
Shadow a complete line and copy the speaker’s rhythm and intonation.
Create a vivid personal association for a word that is hard to remember.
Focus on accuracy first and speed second.
Look for time markers such as yesterday, already, since, and tomorrow.
Practice one grammar skill for several days in a row.
Paraphrase a difficult sentence using simpler English words.
Check that the subject and verb agree before submitting an answer.
Learn words by topic, then mix topics during review.
Write down what you heard and compare it with the transcript.
Do not fear pauses when speaking; a short pause is better than silence.
Repeat the correct version immediately after every mistake.
Create mini-dialogues with new expressions instead of translation lists.
Read examples and try to discover the grammar rule yourself.
Return to your oldest vocabulary cards once a week.
Practice a difficult word syllable by syllable.
Record your voice and compare the stress with a native recording.
Use context to guess an unfamiliar word before opening a dictionary.
In questions, find the auxiliary verb before arranging the words.
Finish each session with one task that makes you feel confident.
Review vocabulary before bed and check it briefly in the morning.
Connect a new grammar rule to a structure you already know.
Describe an object near you with five English adjectives.
Create an affirmative, a question, and a negative example for one tense.
Notice articles while reading and explain why each one is used.
Learn phrasal verbs through short real-life situations.
Compare your answer with the correct one word by word.
Set a small measurable goal: one test and ten minutes of listening.
Rotate grammar, vocabulary, reading, and listening to stay engaged.
Fix one recurring weak point at a time.
Explain a grammar rule in simple words without looking at a textbook.
Write examples about yourself because personal context is memorable.
Before answering, identify the tense and the main subject.
Consistency beats a perfect session, so come back tomorrow.
